Method 3: iQOO's own tools (iQOO Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want iQOO's own route, know what each tool actually does — iQOO has no phone-to-USB backup of its own; the routes on an iQOO phone are iQOO Cloud (vivo Cloud) and Google's, plus PC tools, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. iQOO Cloud Backup is the official cloud backup, powered by vivo's cloud service: sign in with a vivo account and it backs the phone up to vivo's servers — contacts, messages, photos, settings, and app data — and restores them on another iQOO or Vivo phone. It is a real backup — but it lives on vivo's servers, needs a vivo account and a connection, its free storage is limited so a large photo library needs a paid plan, and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. Your iQOO's default gallery app is the Albums app, not Google Photos — but either way it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route the iQOO guides point to first after iQOO Cloud: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. vivo Mobile Assistant is Vivo's PC tool: install it on the computer, connect the phone with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the PC — but that needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. EasyShare is Vivo's phone-switching tool: it moves contacts, messages, photos, and more from an old phone to a new one, or backs the phone up to a PC — but it needs a second phone or a PC on the other end, and it moves data to that device, not to a USB drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — spec tables list OTG for the 13, 12, Neo 10, and Z10 Turbo Pro, but check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, iQOO Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every iQOO phone is confirmed to have OTG — check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); forgetting the OTG switch (on Funtouch OS OTG is off by default, and Vivo's own FAQ says the switch turns itself off if it is not used in 5 minutes — so a drive that worked yesterday can be ignored today; enable it in Settings > More settings > OTG with the drive already attached; if there is no OTG setting at all, the phone may not support OTG); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (iQOO Cloud, Google backup, and Google Photos back your phone up to vivo's or Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup (vivo Mobile Assistant and Coolmuster Android Backup Manager back your iQOO phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on iQOO the cloud routes are iQOO Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up TCL photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/tcl-photos-to-usb.html

TCL phones (50, 40, and 30 series) run TCL UI — TCL's Android skin — with OTG across the current lines: spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the 50 XL NxtPaper and the 50 XE NxtPaper. And TCL has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a TCL phone are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current TCL phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a TCL phone, plug a USB drive in: OTG models mount it straight away with a "USB storage added" notification — TCL UI has no OTG switch to enable, since TCL's own documentation describes no on/off toggle, so there is nothing to turn on first; if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Files works — it is the stock file manager on TCL phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; TCL's own backup routes work too, but TCL has no backup tool of its own, so the routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools like Coolmuster Android Assistant, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive: Google Photos backs photos up to Google's cloud, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from the cloud, and the PC tools back the phone up to a computer. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is a TCL-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a TCL-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the TCL-specific results are cloud and PC backup guides, and the rest are generic manual guides.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up TCL photos to USB drive without computer" and there is no TCL-specific phone-to-USB result in the top results at all — the TCL-specific guides are all cloud or PC routes, and the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com/android-transfer/how-to-transfer-photos-from-android-to-usb.html) — OTG copy, PC drag-and-drop, Google Drive, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; generic Android, and most of the ways need a computer or a cloud account. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — OTG adapter plus its own file manager app, with a progress bar and a FAT32 4 GB warning; generic Android, not written for TCL — and it is a guide for its own app. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=PYcbV25CczI) — a video walkthrough of the generic route: OTG adapter, the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive; generic Android, not written for TCL. softhandtech (softhandtech.com/can-you-transfer-photos-from-phone-to-memory-stick/) — a computer as middleman, direct OTG transfer, or a cloud service; generic Android and iPhone, not written for TCL. thegadgetians (thegadgetians.com/how-to-transfer-files-from-phone-to-usb-without-computer/) — OTG adapter plus the file manager, or a Lightning adapter for iPhones; generic Android and iPhone, not written for TCL. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one-tap app alternative, from the top results for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a TCL guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. mobilespecs.net's TCL 50 XL backup guide (mobilespecs.net/phone/backup/TCL/TCL_50_XL.html) — Google sync (Settings > Google > Synchronization settings, Google Photos for photos), then TWRP Recovery, CWM Recovery + ROM Manager, and Titanium Backup; TCL-specific, but every route is a cloud sync, a custom recovery, or a rooted backup tool — none of them puts plain photo files on a USB drive. mobilespecs.net's TCL 40 X backup guide (mobilespecs.net/phone/backup/TCL/TCL_40_X.html) — the same pattern: Google sync and Google Photos, then TWRP, CWM, and Titanium Backup; TCL-specific, but cloud sync or recovery tools — not a phone-to-USB backup. mobilespecs.net's TCL 40 Pro backup guide (mobilespecs.net/phone/backup/TCL/TCL_40_Pro.html) — the same pattern again: Google sync and Google Photos, then TWRP, CWM, and Titanium Backup; TCL-specific, but cloud sync or recovery tools — not a phone-to-USB backup. mobilespecs.net's TCL 30 V 5G backup guide (mobilespecs.net/phone/backup/TCL/TCL_30_V_5G.html) — the same pattern: Google sync and Google Photos, then TWRP, CWM, and Titanium Backup; TCL-specific, but cloud sync or recovery tools — not a phone-to-USB backup. TCL 30 5G user manual (manualowl.com/m/TCL/30-5G/Manual/689562?page=46) — the manual's own pages: Google Photos "stores and backs up your photos and videos", and Files "displays all data stored on the phone, including both external microSD card and internal storage"; a manual, not a backup guide — but it confirms Google Photos is the stock photo backup and Files is the stock file manager, and the same manual documents OTG and the USB connection setting. TCL's own support FAQ (tcl.com/eu/en/support/faq/37307) — when the phone connects to a PC, pick the mode under Settings > Connections > USB: File transfer, Transfer photos (PTP), No data transfer, or Charge this device; a support FAQ, not a backup guide — but it confirms where TCL puts the USB mode, and that the default is charge-only. Coolmuster's laptop guide (coolmuster.com/android/transfer-photos-from-android-to-laptop.html) — a PC tool (Coolmuster Android Assistant), File Explorer drag-and-drop, Google Photos, or Google Drive; generic Android — TCL appears only in the compatibility list, not as a guide of its own — and every way needs a laptop or a cloud account. TCL 50 XE NxtPaper specs (gsmarena.com.bd/tcl-50-xe-nxtpaper/) — USB Type-C, OTG Yes; Android 14, 128 GB, microSDXC; spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the current TCL 50 line has OTG. TCL 50 XL NxtPaper specs (gsmfind.com/tcl-50-xl-nxtpaper.html) — USB Type-C, OTG; Android 14, 128 GB 6 GB RAM, microSDXC; spec tables, not a guide. Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive. None of them is a TCL-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated TCL photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a TCL phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current TCL phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three TCL specifics: first, OTG is not a given on every model, and TCL UI has no OTG switch to enable. TCL's own documentation describes no on/off toggle — the drive mounts on plug-in — so if a drive never appears, the model may simply not support OTG rather than needing a setting flipped. Spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the 50 XL NxtPaper and the 50 XE NxtPaper, and TCL's own user manual documents OTG on the TCL 30 5G. If the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, TCL ships Google's apps, so the stock file manager is Files — it shows internal storage and the microSD card — and the stock photo backup is Google Photos, which "stores and backs up your photos and videos" per TCL's own manual; TCL camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and most current TCL models have a microSDXC slot (the 50 XL, 50 XE, 40 X, and 30 V 5G all do), so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every model and plugs into any computer as it is. Third, TCL phones sold in the US and Europe ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: TCL's own tools (Google Photos and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want TCL's own route, know what each tool actually does — TCL has no backup tool of its own; the routes on a TCL phone are Google's, plus PC tools, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on TCL — TCL's own manual says Google Photos "stores and backs up your photos and videos": open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route the TCL guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Coolmuster Android Assistant is a PC tool: install it on the computer, connect the phone with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the PC — but that needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. TWRP Recovery and Titanium Backup are the other routes the TCL backup guides list: TWRP is a custom recovery that writes a whole-device backup, and Titanium Backup is a backup tool that needs a rooted phone — both are real backups, but they need a custom recovery or root and a PC or a card to hold the backup, and neither gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — spec tables list OTG for the 50 XL NxtPaper and the 50 XE NxtPaper, and TCL's own manual documents OTG on the 30 5G, but check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every TCL phone is confirmed to have OTG — check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); looking for an OTG switch that isn't there (TCL UI has no OTG toggle in TCL's own documentation — the drive mounts on plug-in, so if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage rather than hunting for a switch; TCL's USB mode setting (Settings > Connections > USB) is for connecting to a computer, not for a drive, and its default is charge-only); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup (Coolmuster Android Assistant backs your TCL phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open); mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but most current TCL models have the slot built in, the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on ZTE — the ZTE backup guides call it "the easiest way" not to lose your photos: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route the ZTE guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Coolmuster Android Assistant and Coolmuster Android Backup Manager are PC tools: install one on the computer, connect the phone with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the PC — but that needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. Samsung Backup and Restore and Samsung Messages Backup are the other PC tools the ZTE guides list: they back the phone up to a computer in one click, with photos among the data types — but again, the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. TWRP Recovery and Titanium Backup are the other routes the ZTE backup guides list: TWRP is a custom recovery that writes a whole-device backup, and Titanium Backup is a backup tool that needs a rooted phone — both are real backups, but they need a custom recovery or root and a PC or a card to hold the backup, and neither gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — spec tables list OTG for the Axon 60, the Axon 60 Ultra, the Axon 30 Ultra, and the Blade V10, but the Blade V30, the Blade V8, the Axon 40 Lite, and the Blade A73 5G have none, so check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (OTG is genuinely mixed across ZTE lines — the Blade V30, the Blade V8, the Axon 40 Lite, and the Blade A73 5G have none — so check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); looking for an OTG switch that isn't there (no OTG toggle turned up in ZTE's own manuals — the drive mounts on plug-in on models that support OTG, so if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage and your model's specs rather than hunting for a switch); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup (Coolmuster Android Assistant, Samsung Backup and Restore, and Samsung Messages Backup back your ZTE phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open); mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but the card slot is mixed across ZTE models (the Axon 60 has one, the Axon 60 Ultra does not), the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on ZTE the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up Fairphone photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/fairphone-photos-to-usb.html

Fairphone phones (4, 5, and 6) run Fairphone OS — near-stock Android — with USB-C and OTG on all three: spec tables list USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG and DisplayPort for the Fairphone 4 and the Fairphone 5, and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Fairphone 6. And Fairphone has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a Fairphone are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools and rooted backup apps, which back your photos up to the cloud, to a computer, or to another device, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Fairphone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any current Fairphone, plug a USB drive in: it mounts straight away with a "USB storage added" notification — Fairphone OS is near-stock Android, so there is no OTG switch to enable and nothing to turn on first; if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: the Files app works — it is the stock file manager on Fairphone OS, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Fairphone's own backup routes work too, but Fairphone has no backup tool of its own, so the routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools like MyPhoneExplorer and rooted apps like Neo Backup, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive: Google Photos backs photos up to Google's cloud, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from the cloud, and the PC tools back the phone up to a computer. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is a Fairphone-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a Fairphone-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the Fairphone-specific results are a forum thread asking how to do it and cloud and PC backup guides, and the rest are generic manual guides.

Search "back up Fairphone photos to USB drive without computer" and there is no Fairphone-specific phone-to-USB guide in the top results at all — the Fairphone-specific result is a forum thread asking how to do it, and the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging: Fairphone community forum, "Back up on hard disk" (Back up on hard disk - Fairphone 5) — a Fairphone 5 owner asking how to back up to an offline disk instead of Google One. The answers are Swift Backup, Syncthing to sync photos with other devices, Neo Backup (needs root), FolderSync to a USB drive, MyPhoneExplorer (a PC tool), or a USB cable to a PC — a discussion, not a guide. One reply says "go into your settings (choose Backup), plug in a USB type C external drive and do a manual backup" — but that reply is about LineageOS, not Fairphone OS, as the next reply in the thread points out. Nobody in the thread gives a Fairphone-specific phone-to-USB photo backup.; YouTube (How to Connect USB Drive to Android Phone to Move Photos & Videos) — a video walkthrough of the generic route: OTG adapter, the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive. Generic Android, not written for Fairphone.; FotoSafe (Back up Android photos to USB) — connect the drive, select it in FotoSafe, review the media and start copying. Generic Android, not written for Fairphone — and it is a guide for its own app.; Dr.Fone (4 Practical Ways to Transfer Photos from Android to USB Flash Drive) — OTG copy, PC drag-and-drop, Google Drive, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi. Generic Android, and most of the ways need a computer or a cloud account.; AnExplorer (USB OTG File Manager for Android — Read, Write, Transfer) — plug a USB drive in via OTG and AnExplorer gives full read/write access, with FAT32, exFAT, and NTFS support. Generic Android, not written for Fairphone — and it is a guide for its own app.; softhandtech (Transfer Photos from Phone to Memory Stick: A Comprehensive Guide) — a computer as middleman, direct OTG transfer, or a cloud service. Generic Android and iPhone, not written for Fairphone.; Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Google Play) — the one-tap app alternative, from the top results for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a Fairphone guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; Fairphone community forum, "Backup your phone" guide (Backup your phone - Guides) — Fairphone's own community guide: TWRP custom recovery, CWM custom recovery, Titanium Backup (needs root), the built-in backup app, or Google sync to the cloud. Fairphone-specific, but every route is a custom recovery, a rooted backup tool, or a cloud sync — none of them puts plain photo files on a USB drive.; Fairphone community forum, "How to do a full backup when rooted?" (How to do a full backup when rooted?) — the thread's own conclusion: the only official backup way is sending all data to Google, and without root there is nothing like a full backup; the suggestions are Neo Backup, Swift Backup, and TWRP, which the thread notes has not been updated for years. Fairphone-specific, but rooted tools and Google's cloud — not a phone-to-USB photo backup.; /e/OS community, "How do I back up my Fairphone 6 with /e/OS?" (How do I back up my Fairphone 6 with /e/OS?) — for the de-Googled Fairphone 6, the backup is Seedvault (Settings > System > Backup > Seedvault), with the backup destination set to the SD card. Fairphone-specific, but it backs up apps and data to a card, not a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.; Fairphone support, "How to back up or restore data on your Fairphone" (How to back up or restore data on your Fairphone) — Fairphone's own support page, and the only backup way it presents is Google backup: the thread on the forum confirms "the Google backup is certainly presented as the official way for backing up a Fairphone" and "there are no other ways mentioned in the official docs". Fairphone-specific, but it backs the phone up to Google's cloud — not to a USB drive.; Technobezz's Fairphone 5 data transfer guide (Fairphone 5 Data Transfer Guide) — wireless "Copy your data" during setup, a USB cable to the old phone, or restore from a Google One backup (Settings > System > Backup). Fairphone-specific, but it moves data to a new phone or restores it from Google's cloud — not a phone-to-USB photo backup.; Fairphone 5 specs (Fairphone 5) — USB-C 3.0 (DisplayPort, USB-OTG); microSDXC (dedicated slot). Spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Fairphone 5 has OTG. The same page notes the Fairphone 5 was discontinued in January 2026.; Fairphone 4 specs (Fairphone 4) — USB-C 3.0 (DisplayPort, USB-OTG); microSD up to 2 TB. Spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Fairphone 4 has OTG.; Fairphone 6 specs (Fairphone 6) — USB Type-C 2.0, OTG; microSDXC (dedicated slot); Android 15 with up to 8 major Android upgrades. Spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the current Fairphone 6 has OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Fairphone-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Fairphone photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: A Fairphone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Fairphone 4, 5, and 6 all have USB-C with OTG, so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive; a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Fairphone specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current models — spec tables list USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG and DisplayPort for the Fairphone 4 and the Fairphone 5, and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Fairphone 6 — and Fairphone OS is near-stock Android with no OTG switch, so the drive mounts on plug-in; if the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, Fairphone ships the Files app as the stock file manager — Fairphone owners in the community forum copy pictures, videos, and audio "with Files app to the SD card" — and the stock photo backup is Google Photos, which is the route Fairphone's own support page presents; Fairphone camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and every current Fairphone has a dedicated microSDXC slot (up to 2 TB), so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, Fairphone OS ships with Google apps including the Play Store, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — the one exception is the /e/OS Fairphone 6, which has no Play Store, so the APK is the install route there. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Fairphone's own tools (Google Photos and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want Fairphone's own route, know what each tool actually does — Fairphone has no backup tool of its own; the routes on a Fairphone are Google's, plus PC tools and rooted apps, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Fairphone — Fairphone's own support page presents Google backup as the official way to back up a Fairphone: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route Fairphone's support page points to: Settings > System > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Seedvault is the backup on the /e/OS Fairphone 6: Settings > System > Backup > Seedvault, with the backup destination set to the SD card — it backs up apps and data to a card, but not a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive, and the /e/OS community notes quite a few things are excluded. MyPhoneExplorer is a PC tool: install it on the computer, connect the phone with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the PC — but that needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. Swift Backup and FolderSync are the other tools the Fairphone forum suggests: Swift Backup backs apps and data up to a card or to a cloud, and FolderSync syncs files to a USB drive or anywhere else — but Swift Backup needs root-level access (Shizuku) for a full backup, and FolderSync is a sync tool you configure yourself, not a one-tap photo backup. Neo Backup and Titanium Backup are the other routes the Fairphone guides list: both need a rooted phone — and the forum thread notes TWRP has not been updated for years and no longer works with current encryption. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

Three Sharp specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current models — spec tables list USB Type-C 3.2 with OTG for the Aquos R10 and the Aquos sense9, and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Aquos R9 — and Sharp runs near-stock Android with no OTG switch, so the drive mounts on plug-in; if the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, Sharp ships Files by Google as the stock file manager — Sharp's own FAQ pages point to the Files app for finding downloaded files — and the stock photo backup is Google Photos, which is the route Sharp's own FAQ pages present; Sharp camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and every current Aquos has a microSDXC slot, so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, Sharp phones ship with Google apps including the Play Store, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Sharp's own tools (Google Photos and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want Sharp's own route, know what each tool actually does — Sharp has no backup tool of its own; the routes on a Sharp Aquos are Google's, plus docomo Data Copy on Japan carrier models, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Sharp — Sharp's own FAQ pages present Google Photos as the route for backing up photos and videos: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the other Google route: Settings > System > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. docomo Data Copy is the backup on Japan carrier models: it copies phonebook, mail, and media to a microSD card, or directly to another phone over a one-to-one connection — but that backs the phone up to a card or another phone, not to a USB drive. Data Storage Box is the same carrier route for call log and music. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; Older Sharp models use micro-USB. The Aquos Zeta SH-01H and other older models have a micro-USB port, so a USB-C drive or adapter will not fit — a micro-USB OTG adapter is the route there. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Aquos — the Aquos R10, R9, and sense9 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Looking for an OTG switch that isn't there. Sharp runs near-stock Android with no OTG toggle — the drive mounts on plug-in, so if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage rather than hunting for a switch.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool.; Mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup. Sharp's own manuals back your Aquos up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.; Mistaking a carrier backup for a USB backup. docomo Data Copy backs your Aquos up to a microSD card or another phone — a real backup, but it lands on the card or the other phone, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — every current Aquos has a microSDXC slot — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Sharp the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

No computer, no upload, no account. A discontinued PC app, not a phone-to-USB copy.; Wondershare MobileTrans, "HTC Backup App: An Ultimate Guide and Best Alternatives" (HTC Backup App: An Ultimate Guide and Best Alternatives) — HTC Sync Manager is a freely available desktop application from HTC that backs up and restores data to a PC, and the HTC Backup app backs up to an HTC or Google account. Both routes land on a PC or in a cloud account — neither writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive.; AnExplorer (USB OTG File Manager for Android — Read, Write, Transfer) — plug a USB drive in via OTG and AnExplorer gives full read/write access, with FAT32, exFAT, and NTFS support. Generic Android, not written for HTC — and it is a guide for its own app.; Dr.Fone (4 Practical Ways to Transfer Photos from Android to USB Flash Drive) — OTG copy, PC drag-and-drop, Google Drive, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not an HTC guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; HTC U23 Pro vs HTC Desire 22 Pro specs (HTC U23 Pro vs HTC Desire 22 Pro) — USB-C v3.0 with USB on-the-go for the U23 Pro, USB-C v2.0 with USB on-the-go for the Desire 22 Pro. Spec tables, not a guide — and the confirmation that the U23 has OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is an HTC-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated HTC photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: An HTC phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the U23 Pro has USB-C 3.0 with OTG, the Desire 22 Pro has USB-C 2.0 with OTG, and the U23 has USB-C 3.0 with OTG — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three HTC specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current models — spec tables list USB-C with OTG for the U23 Pro, the Desire 22 Pro, and the U23 — and HTC's own support pages for the U12+ and the U12 life say the same thing in HTC's own words: connect an OTG connector, go to Settings > Storage, and tap the name of the drive. Second, HTC's own backup tool is a desktop app — HTC Sync Manager backs your pictures, videos, and more up to a PC — and it is discontinued, support ended; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; HTC camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and the U23 Pro and the Desire 22 Pro both have a microSDXC slot, so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, and the HTC One has no microSD slot at all; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: HTC's own tools (HTC Sync Manager, HTC Backup, Google Photos, Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want HTC's own route, know what each tool actually does — HTC's own backup tool is a desktop app, and it is discontinued, and the other routes are Google's, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. HTC Sync Manager is HTC's own tool for HTC phones — but it is a Windows and Mac desktop application: connect the phone to a PC with a USB cable, and its Transfer & Backup backs up the pictures, videos, music, contacts, and more of your device to the computer and restores them later. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files, and it is discontinued: support has ended and it will never be updated, so continuing to use it risks sync errors or data loss. HTC Backup is HTC's own phone app — but it backs up to an HTC or Google account, which is a cloud backup, not a USB copy. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on HTC phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the other Google route: Settings > System > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; Older HTC models use micro-USB. The HTC One and other older models have a micro-USB port, so a USB-C drive or adapter will not fit — a micro-USB OTG adapter is the route there. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current HTC — the U23 Pro, Desire 22 Pro, and U23 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, or for the micro-USB HTC One.; Looking for an OTG switch that may not be there. On most HTC phones the drive mounts on plug-in — if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage and tap the name of the drive, as HTC's own support pages describe, rather than hunting for a switch.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. HTC Sync Manager backs your HTC phone up — but it is a desktop app, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool.; Mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup. HTC Sync Manager backs your HTC phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.; Trusting a discontinued tool with your only copy. HTC Sync Manager has been discontinued and support has ended — it still installs, but it will never be updated, and its sync engine should be treated with caution. Do not make it your only backup.; Mistaking a storage-expansion guide for a backup guide. The HTC One guide about expanding storage with a USB OTG cable is about opening files stored on the drive — it is not a guide for copying your camera roll to the drive.; Mistaking an OTG support page for a backup guide. HTC's own U12+ and U12 life pages explain how to view files from a USB drive — they do not back anything up. Viewing is not copying.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — the U23 Pro and the Desire 22 Pro both have a microSDXC slot — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. The HTC One has no microSD slot at all.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On HTC the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Blackview photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Blackview rugged phones (BV9300, BV9300 Pro, and BV6200 Pro) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the BV9300, OTG reverse charging for the BV9300 Pro, and OTG for the BV6200 Pro — and Blackview's own backup guide lists USB OTG as an external-storage option you can copy files to by hand. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Blackview. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

No computer, no upload, no account. Method 3: Blackview's own tools (the 6 ways, Google Photos, Google backup, Data Migration — not phone-to-USB). If you want Blackview's own route, know what each tool actually does — Blackview's own backup guide is six generic Android ways, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Account Backup is Blackview's own first way — Settings > Google > Backup, "Back up to Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage, which Blackview's own guide says may not be sufficient for photos and videos. 2. Local Backup to Computer is Blackview's own second way — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable, open File Explorer or Finder, and copy the files to the computer's local storage or an external hard drive. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 3. Third-party backup apps is Blackview's own third way — Google One, Dropbox, MEGA, Box, Samsung Smart Switch, OneDrive, and Titanium Backup (which needs root). They are real backups — but they are cloud apps or a PC tool, not a phone-to-USB copy, and Blackview's own guide tells you to review each app's privacy policy before trusting it with your data. 4. Backup to External Storage is Blackview's own fourth way — "many Android phones support the use of a microSD card or USB OTG storage — you can use these external storage options to manually copy your important files, photos, and other data for a local backup." It is the closest thing in Blackview's own guide to this article's job — but it is a manual copy, and the manual copy is Method 2 above. 5. ADB backup is Blackview's own fifth way — enable Developer Options and USB Debugging, install Android Platform Tools on a computer, connect the phone, and run the ADB backup command. It is a real backup — but it needs a computer and command-line tools, and some apps block ADB backups. 6. Custom recovery is Blackview's own sixth way — unlock the bootloader, install TWRP, and create a full system image. It is a real backup — but it is expert level, and Blackview's own guide says it may void warranties or risk data loss if done incorrectly. Data Migration is Blackview's phone-to-phone tool — a few taps transfer all your data from an old device to a new one. It is a real transfer — but it moves data to a new phone, not to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Blackview phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the per-model backup guides say the most economical backup is to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Ulefone's own backup routes work too, but they are Google backup and Google Photos, which back your photos up to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Generic Android, and two of the three ways need a computer or a cloud account.; Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Google Play) — the one-tap app alternative, known from earlier scoring of this niche (it did not surface in this query's top results): a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a Ulefone guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; Ulefone Armor 28 Ultra specs (UleFone Armor 28 Ultra 16GB/1TB Black) — "with fast charging and OTG support", 1 TB of storage, a TF card slot. A retailer spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Armor 28 Ultra has OTG.; Ulefone Armor 34 Pro specs (UleFone Armor 34 Pro 16GB/512GB Pulse Black) — Functions list includes OTG, Android 15, 512 GB of storage, a TF card slot. A retailer spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Armor 34 Pro has OTG.; Ulefone Armor 27 Pro specs (Ulefone Armor 27 Pro) — "USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG support", 256 GB of storage. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Armor 27 Pro has OTG.; Ulefone Armor Mini 20 specs (Ulefone Armor Mini 20) — storage "expandable via USB OTG", USB Type-C 2.0, 256 GB of storage. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Armor Mini 20 supports USB OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Ulefone-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Ulefone photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: A Ulefone phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Armor 28 Ultra lists OTG support, the Armor 34 Pro lists OTG among its functions, the Armor 27 Pro has USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the Armor Mini 20 expands storage via USB OTG — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Ulefone specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current Armor models — spec tables list OTG support for the Armor 28 Ultra and the Armor 34 Pro, USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Armor 27 Pro, and USB OTG expansion for the Armor Mini 20. Second, Ulefone has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the per-model backup guides all point to the same three things: connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, back up to Google Drive, or use Google Photos for photos — with TWRP, CWM, and Titanium Backup (root) for experts; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Ulefone camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The Armor 28 Ultra and the Armor 28 Pro both have a TF card slot — on the Armor 28 Pro the TF card slot is separate from the SIM tray — so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Ulefone's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, per-model FAQ guides — not phone-to-USB). If you want Ulefone's own route, know what each tool actually does — the per-model backup guides for the Armor 25T, Armor Pad, Armor 27T, Armor 2S, Armor 2, Power 3L, Power Armor 18 Ultra, and MIX all point to the same three things, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the guides describe — Settings > System > Backup, "Back up to Google Drive" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Ulefone phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is what the per-model guides call the most economical method — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. TWRP Recovery, CWM Recovery, and Titanium Backup are the expert methods the per-model guides list — a modified recovery environment that creates a full system backup, or a system backup tool that needs root. They are real backups — but they are expert level, need an unlocked bootloader or root, and may void warranties. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The TF card slot is separate on the Armor 28 Pro. The Armor 28 Pro's TF card slot is separate from the SIM tray, so a card and a second SIM do not compete for the same tray — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Ulefone — the Armor 28 Ultra, Armor 34 Pro, Armor 27 Pro, and Armor Mini 20 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The per-model backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model FAQ for a phone-to-USB guide. The devicesfaq and mobilespecs pages for the Armor 25T, Armor Pad, Armor 27T, and the rest are real Ulefone backup pages — but their backup advice is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with TWRP and Titanium Backup for experts. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking an expert tool for a photo backup. TWRP Recovery needs an unlocked bootloader, and Titanium Backup needs root — the per-model guides list both as expert methods. Neither is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive.; Mistaking a TF-card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a TF card is a real local copy — the Armor 28 Ultra and the Armor 28 Pro both have a TF card slot — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. The Armor 27 Pro has no microSD card support mentioned at all.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Ulefone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Doogee photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Doogee rugged phones (S118 Pro, S118, and S98) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S118 Pro, the S118 Pro manual lists OTG with reverse charging, and the S98 lists On-The-Go among its USB features — and Doogee has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Doogee the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up CAT photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/cat-photos-to-usb.html

CAT rugged phones (S75, S62 Pro, and S53) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S75 and the S62 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG for the S53 — and CAT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current CAT. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any USB-C CAT, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the S75 and the S62 Pro list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the S53 lists USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the per-model backup guides say the most economical backup is to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; CAT's own backup routes work too, but they are Google backup and Google Photos, which back your photos up to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is a CAT-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a CAT-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the CAT-specific results are per-model FAQ pages whose backup advice is a computer copy or a cloud backup, and the rest are generic manual guides.
