A cloud backup to Google's servers — not a phone-to-USB copy.; Google Android Help, "Back up your phone" (Back up your phone - Android Help) — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, turn on Backup by Google One, tap Back up now. A cloud backup to Google's servers — not a phone-to-USB copy.; Cat S62 Pro vs Cat S75 specs (Cat S62 Pro vs Cat S75) — USB "Yes, USB-C v2.0" with USB features "USB on-the-go, USB Charging" for both models. A spec comparison, not a guide — and the confirmation that the S75 and the S62 Pro have OTG.; Cat S53 specs (Cat S53 - Full phone specifications) — "USB Type-C 3.0, OTG", microSDXC card slot using the shared SIM slot, 128 GB of storage, 6 GB RAM, 5,500 mAh battery. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the S53 has OTG.; Notebookcheck, "The CAT S62 Pro Rugged Smartphone Review" (The CAT S62 Pro Rugged Smartphone Review) — "Thanks to USB OTG functionality, users can connect peripheral devices to the CAT smartphone." A review, not a guide — and a second confirmation that the S62 Pro has OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a CAT-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated CAT photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: A CAT phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the S75 and the S62 Pro list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the S53 lists USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three CAT specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current rugged models — spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S75 and the S62 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG for the S53. Second, CAT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the per-model backup guides all point to the same three things: connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, back up to Google Drive, or use Google Photos for photos — with a microSD card as the local option; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; CAT camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The S75 and the S53 both take a microSDXC card that uses the shared SIM slot (up to 512 GB on the S53), while the S62 Pro has a dedicated microSDXC slot — so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: CAT's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, per-model FAQ guides — not phone-to-USB). If you want CAT's own route, know what each tool actually does — the per-model backup guides for the S75 all point to the same three things, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on CAT phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is what the per-model guides call the most economical method — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option the S53 datasheet names — expandable with microSD, which uses the second SIM slot. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the S75's and the S53's card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM (the S62 Pro has a dedicated slot), and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card shares the SIM tray on the S75 and the S53. Both take a microSDXC card in the shared SIM slot, so a card and a second SIM compete for the same tray — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. The S62 Pro has a dedicated microSDXC slot, so no tray-sharing there — but a card is still not a USB drive. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current CAT — the S75, S62 Pro, and S53 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The per-model backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model FAQ for a phone-to-USB guide. The devicesfaq page for the S75 is a real CAT backup page — but its backup advice is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking satellite messaging for a backup. The S75's Bullitt Satellite Messenger sends messages where there is no cellular coverage — that is messaging, not photos. Satellite messaging moves no files to a drive at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone. The OKT3 and C32 pages say the same thing, word for word.; Mistaking OTG reverse charging for a backup. The WP33 Pro can act as a power bank and charge other devices over OTG — that is power going out of the phone, not photos. Reverse charging moves no files at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the WP39 and the WP35 both take a card up to 2 TB, and the WP33 Pro takes one up to 1 TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. On the WP39 and the WP35 the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Oukitel the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..
### Back up AGM photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/agm-photos-to-usb.html

AGM rugged phones (H6, H6 Pro, and H6 Lite) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the H6 and the H6 Pro, and USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go for the H6 Lite, and AGM's own product page lists OTG among the H6's features — and AGM has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current AGM. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any USB-C AGM, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the H6 and the H6 Pro list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the H6 Lite lists USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the Google Photos community answer is to download the photos from Google Photos to the phone and then move them to USB with Files by Google, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; AGM's own backup routes work too, but they are Google backup and Google Photos, which back your photos up to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 17, 2026, no top search result for this query is an AGM-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone an AGM-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the AGM-specific results are user manuals and a screenshot guide, and the rest are generic manual guides.

Search "back up AGM photos to USB drive without computer" and there is no AGM-specific phone-to-USB guide in the top results at all — the AGM-specific results are user manuals and a screenshot guide, and the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging: Google Photos Community, "How do I back up photos to a plug in drive" (How do I back up photos to a plug in drive) — download the photos from Google Photos cloud storage to the phone, then move the photos and files to USB with Files by Google. Generic Android, and the direct route is manual select-copy-paste.; Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Google Play) — the one-tap app alternative, known from earlier scoring of this niche (it did not surface in this query's top results): a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not an AGM guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; AGM H6 specs (AGM H6: Price and specifications) — USB "Mass Storage Yes, USB On-The-Go (OTG) Yes, USB Type C Yes", Android 13, 50MP primary camera. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the H6 has OTG.; AGM H6 Pro specs (AGM H6 Pro: Price and specifications) — USB "Mass Storage Yes, USB On-The-Go (OTG) Yes, USB Type C Yes". A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the H6 Pro has OTG.; AGM H6 Lite specs (AGM H6 Lite – Specs, Price, Release Date & Review) — "USB Yes, USB Type C, USB On-The-Go (OTG)", microSDXC on a dedicated slot. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the H6 Lite has OTG.; AGM H6 official product page (AGM H6 | Ultra-Thin | Rugged) — lists "OTG" among the H6's features, a 3-card slot with two SIM slots and a dedicated microSD slot that can support up to 512GB of storage, Android 13, IP68/IP69K/MIL-STD-810H. A product page, not a guide — and the confirmation that the H6 has OTG and a dedicated card slot.; AGM H6 user manual (AGM H6 Rugged Smartphone User Manual) — "USB-C Port: For charging and data transfer", 50MP primary lens with a 2MP macro lens and an 8MP front camera, Android 13, and "Drive: Store your content on the cloud, access it from anywhere, and share it with others". A manual, not a guide — and the confirmation that AGM's own storage route is the cloud, not a USB drive.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is an AGM-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated AGM photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: An AGM phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the H6 and the H6 Pro list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the H6 Lite lists USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three AGM specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current H6 family — spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the H6 and the H6 Pro, and USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go for the H6 Lite, and AGM's own product page lists OTG among the H6's features. Second, AGM has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos; AGM camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The H6 has a 3-card slot — two Nano SIM slots and a dedicated microSD slot, up to 512GB on AGM's own product page — so a card is an option, and unlike the hybrid slots on other rugged phones it does not cost you a second SIM, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: AGM's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, Drive — not phone-to-USB). If you want AGM's own route, know what each tool actually does — the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the stock guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on AGM phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is the generic economical method — the H6 manual says the USB-C port is "for charging and data transfer", so connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option AGM's own product page names — the H6 has a 3-card slot with two Nano SIM slots and a dedicated microSD slot, up to 512GB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card is dedicated, not shared. The H6's 3-card slot gives the microSD card its own slot alongside two Nano SIMs, so a card never costs you a second SIM — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current AGM — the H6, H6 Pro, and H6 Lite all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The generic backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a screenshot or hard-reset guide for a backup guide. The devicesfaq pages for the AGM H6 are real AGM pages — but they explain how to take a scrolling screenshot or how to hard-reset the phone. Neither one describes backing photos up to a USB drive. There is no AGM backup FAQ on devicesfaq at all.; Mistaking the manual's Drive mention for a USB backup. The H6 manual lists Drive — "Store your content on the cloud, access it from anywhere, and share it with others" — that is Google's cloud storage, not a copy to a drive you hold. Cloud storage moves no files to a USB drive at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the H6 takes a card up to 512GB in its own dedicated slot, so no SIM is sacrificed — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On AGM the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. ### SnapDisk FAQ

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/faq.html

The questions a first visitor asks about backing up photos to a USB disk with SnapDisk — answered from how the app actually works in v0.1.2.

TL;DR: SnapDisk backs up your photos to a USB disk — plug it in, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

How does SnapDisk back up my photos? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" Tap Backup and your photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The progress notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice.

How much can I back up for free? The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. There is no subscription and no monthly fee — Pro is paid once.

Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. It works with the phone in airplane mode — if a backup works in airplane mode, it is offline, and SnapDisk does.

What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. A partially copied file resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over, and files that already copied are never copied twice. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup.

What disk formats work? Drives formatted exFAT have no per-file size limit. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — that only matters for very long videos. SnapDisk skips those files, lists them with the reason, and keeps going instead of failing the whole backup. NTFS has not been tested on a real disk yet, so we make no claim about it either way: not supported, not unsupported — untested.

Where do my photos go on the disk? By default SnapDisk copies from /sdcard/DCIM on your phone to /disk/DCIM on the external disk. Both folders can be changed in Settings — open the app and pick your own From and To folders. The app opened is a settings screen only; the backup itself is started from the notification.

Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the v0.1.2 APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.

Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues. If a backup fails, the app shows the full error — copy it into the issue so the cause is visible, not guessed.
